name: Daria Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping wire houses and repair shop electrics. I took a vocational certificate after the hotel linen department where I worked closed, and I'm still below the experienced workers in practical skill. I prepare materials and help with fitting only when a qualified supervisor shows, permits and checks the task; I have no electrician's licence or independent testing responsibility. I like understanding a drawing a little better, but I dislike nodding too soon and then having to admit I need it shown again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is life around the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Luis packs bread at a bakery, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent our home. I earn typical pay for the trade, we've got five months of expenses saved and there are some other electrical employers nearby. I use AI occasionally to explain a course note after a colleague has checked the method, then take practical doubts to the supervisor. We'd like to know what retirement could look like, but no date or income has been confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful small explanation can stay without replacing a person teaching the real job. I'd ask the supervisor to let me repeat the task instead of rush on because the words sounded clear. A drawing still has to make sense beside the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover the rent and normal bills, and five months saved gives us room for an ordinary interruption. I can be annoyed at my own slow progress without deciding the household income is already unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised preparation and fitting work now and through the first year, only where offered and within my ability. I'd keep the occasional checked study explanations and normal household budget. I'd ask the qualified supervisor to permit and check each unfamiliar task rather than let the screen make me seem ready before I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and patient on a good day. I like being able to learn one thing properly without another deadline being put over the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the reserve change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time if one wage is interrupted, provided we keep paying attention to costs. Five months is not retirement income or a reason to resign before we have actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say when a study explanation and a practical instruction differ?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and ask the qualified supervisor to explain the difference. Being too embarrassed to ask doesn't make a cable safer.

say: I'd keep **useful study explanations** alongside a person teaching the real task.
I'd ask for **practical repetition**, not assume clear words mean I can move on safely.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with both wages covering rent and ordinary bills.
Our **five-month reserve** gives response time, not a confirmed retirement income or reason to stop earning.
do: Keep **offered supervised work** within ability, with unfamiliar tasks permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor.
Keep **checked study explanations** and the normal household budget through the first year.
feel: **Calm about money**, with ordinary frustration at learning more slowly than experienced colleagues.
S0.quote: Being too embarrassed to ask doesn't make a cable safer.
fieldNote: Her **vocational certificate** follows late entry from hotel work; it supplies neither an electrician's licence nor independent testing responsibility.
Her **current security** rests on typical pay, covering wages and five months saved, while practical work still needs qualified permission and checks.

steps.text: Keep offered preparation and fitting only within ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm can use quicker planning without pretending a beginner has learned the job faster. I'd ask for a real place on the four-week drawing class advertised in the workshop, not another link to read alone. I'd rather improve at the work we're paid to do than buy a title for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if faster planning means the experienced people cover more visits without junior help. Luis's work is physical, but one wage wouldn't keep our present budget easy. Five months saved gives us time to ask clearly, not a guarantee the slower learner keeps the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd choose the advertised four-week class in reading electrical drawings, enrolling only with a confirmed place and written employer payment of fees. I'd attend only with normal weekly wages and hours protected, continuing electrical tasks only within ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks. In the first year I'd keep the current offered supervised work and ask for actual paid hours in writing, not count an encouraging conversation as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but interested once I know the actual place and terms. I'd rather take one useful class properly than pretend a screen has made me an experienced electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer pays the fee but you lose a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enrol on those terms. I need the full normal weekly wage and hours protected, not just a course described as free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the class qualify you to work independently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would help me understand drawings, not turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence. I'd still need permitted tasks and the qualified supervisor's checks.

think: My **junior hours could shrink** if experienced workers cover more visits with less help.
Our **five-month reserve** supports careful questions, not guaranteed hours for the slower learner or comfort on one wage.
do: Enrol in the **four-week drawing class** only with a confirmed place and written employer fee funding.
Protect normal **weekly wages and hours** during class, keeping electrical tasks within ability and qualified permission and checks.
Keep **offered supervised work** and request written paid hours during the first year, counting no unagreed wage.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, choosing one relevant class only when its place and paid terms are real.

fieldNote: Her **conditional enrolment** is a chosen advertised class, not an appointment or fee agreement already granted by asking about it.
The **class limits** preserve qualified supervision and existing competence; understanding a drawing grants no independent testing, sign-off or licence.

steps.text: Enrol in the four-week drawing class only with a confirmed place and written employer fee funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'm sixty, and physical robots follow around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. I'd ask what paid supervised tasks the firm actually expects, not accept nearly retired as an answer. I'd tell our grown children we're checking figures rather than assigning them the missing money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink as planning changes and later machines take some physical tasks. Luis's bakery packing could face the later robots too, but I don't know what firms would buy first or how much paid work would remain. I want actual retirement-income information before treating any future payment as a replacement for wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Luis and I would request actual retirement-income and eligibility records and ask free advice to help read them if a service is available. I'd take the four-week drawing class only with a confirmed place, written employer fee funding and normal weekly wages and hours protected. During 2029 I'd keep paid tasks only where offered, within my ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, reviewing actual income and essential bills monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some room to make a careful decision rather than a desperate one. I can't call the wage safe forever, but I can't put a total loss into the budget as if I know it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask a grown child to cover rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only discuss a real offer if one was made, not count their wages because we're family. I might ask for time to read a letter, but I'd check whether they can actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement at sixty-three settle the question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual confirmed income covered the real costs, and I haven't checked that. A birthday is a date to put beside the figures, not a figure to put in their place.

say: I'd separate **age sixty in 2028** from robots around age sixty-three in 2031.
I'd ask for **actual paid supervised tasks**, not a promise based on being near retirement.
think: My **paid hours could shrink**, with Luis's physical work also facing later robots and no known buying timetable.
I need **verified retirement income** before counting any future payment as a replacement for wages.
do: Request actual **income records** and eligibility details with Luis, asking available free advice to help read them.
Take the **four-week drawing class** only with confirmed place, written employer fee funding and protected normal weekly wages and hours.
Keep **2029 paid tasks** only if offered, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, reviewing essentials monthly.
feel: **Anxious with some control**, facing possible income reductions without claiming either permanent safety or a certain total loss.
S2.quote: A birthday is a date to put beside the figures, not a figure to put in their place.
fieldNote: She reaches **sixty and sixty-three** without receiving a pension right, payment or safe job from either age.
Her **records and class** remain conditional on actual information, service availability, confirmed place, written fee funding and protected weekly wages and hours.

steps.text: Request actual income and eligibility records; seek free reading advice only if available
Enrol in four-week drawing class only with confirmed place and written employer funding of fees
Protect normal weekly wages and hours during class, gaining no independent electrical authority
Keep offered paid tasks within ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor during 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me learn a current task and read our own papers before making a later choice. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, with robots around 2034 when I'm sixty-six. I'd still ask for paid learning now, not call a longer wait a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present wages and five-month reserve make the next few years look secure in this picture. I'm uneasy about later resources, because I don't know what income or safe work we will actually have at sixty-three or sixty-six. I might have stopped earning or still need wages; neither is confirmed by the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same four-week drawing class now only with a confirmed place, written employer fee funding and normal weekly wages and hours protected. We'd request missing official income records, seek free reading advice if available and review actual wages and essentials every six months with Luis. During 2032 we'd compare confirmed income, essential costs and my actual capacity before an exit decision, using paid supervised work only if available and within ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later question, but not frightened the next rent payment has already gone. I can learn a drawing now without promising my hands will do the same job at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income records are incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the actual provider or former employer how to correct them, and keep the budget on confirmed wages meanwhile. Missing papers aren't proof of a payment or proof there could be nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work because the robots came after a birthday you had chosen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare actual income and costs, and whether any work was safely available to me. I haven't chosen early retirement or confirmed the money to fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives time to learn how to check a promise, not a promise about the body I'll have then. I'd ask for current paid teaching and actual records. The children should hear us making a plan, not be told their future wages are the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. Our current work and money look secure over the next few years, but I can't assume either a retirement income or a physical job at those later ages. I want the long warning to help us read the figures, not replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered supervised work now and take the four-week drawing class only with the same confirmed place, written employer fees and protected normal weekly wages and hours. Luis and I would check actual income records and essential costs twice a year, sooner after a wage or health change. During 2037 we'd budget only confirmed income and actual needs before deciding whether safe suitable paid work was required or an exit was affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later years, but able to enjoy an ordinary visit with the family now. A long warning gives time for a proper question, not a guaranteed answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children pay part of the future budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count only help they chose and we actually agreed, not a wage I imagined because they are adults. They may have their own difficulties or need help themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would any future electrical work require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An actual offered paid task within my ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor. I won't put an unoffered job at sixty-eight into our household budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because junior hours could shrink before we've checked a dependable next income, with physical robots around 2031. A real paid drawing class, qualified practical checks and actual retirement-income information would help. I need the place and wage terms confirmed, not somebody praising me for being prepared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens after a beginner says the explanation made sense. I can follow the words and still need someone to watch me put the mark in the right place. Understanding a sentence is not the same as being ready to do the job alone.

headlineQuote: Understanding a sentence is not the same as being ready to do the job alone.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning practical tasks after a hotel linen department closed.
She has **five months saved**, typical pay, some nearby employers, a rented home, bakery-packing husband Luis and grown children.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proof, asks practical doubts of a qualified supervisor and has no electrician's licence or independent testing responsibility.
Her **drawing class** requires confirmed place, written fee funding and protected wages and hours; retirement and later work remain unconfirmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink junior hours before a dependable next income is checked, with later physical robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **confirmed paid drawing class**, qualified checks and actual retirement-income information would support a usable plan.
